opus-5.5.text:
I think so, but I'd frame it carefully, because "efficiency" means a few different things.

If you mean sample efficiency, how many examples it takes to learn something, then biology is still way ahead in a lot of domains. A child picks up a new word from a handful of exposures, and our models need orders of magnitude more data to get comparable robustness. But it's not really a fair fight. Evolution spent hundreds of millions of years doing a kind of outer-loop optimization. It baked in priors, architecture, and learning rules, so what looks like learning from five examples is really learning from five examples plus a few billion years of pretraining. When you account for that, the gap looks less mysterious.

If you mean energy efficiency, the brain running on roughly twenty watts, that's a hardware and substrate question as much as an algorithms question. I think we'll make big gains there, but it's a different engineering problem.

What makes me optimistic is that we've barely started optimizing for efficiency. For most of the last decade the recipe was "scale works, so scale." Compute was the lever, and data was abundant enough that nobody had to be clever about squeezing more out of each token. That's changing. We're running into the limits of high-quality data, so there's real pressure now on better optimizers, better curricula, better ways of reusing data, and models that generate and verify their own training signal. My own bias, having worked a lot on optimization, is that there's a lot of slack left in how we train. Second-order methods, smarter preconditioning, better use of each gradient step: none of that is free, but it's underexplored relative to its potential.

There's also a structural advantage artificial systems have that biology doesn't. Models can share what they've learned directly. You can copy weights, distill, merge, and run thousands of copies gathering experience in parallel. A human has to relearn everything from scratch every generation. So even if a single model is less sample-efficient than a single brain, the system as a whole can be dramatically more efficient at accumulating knowledge.

So my answer is: in narrow, well-specified domains we've arguably already passed it. On the broad, flexible, learn-from-very-little kind of efficiency, we're not there yet, but I don't see a fundamental barrier. It's an engineering and research problem, and those tend to yield once enough smart people are pointed at them.

r001.rationale: The response says broad, flexible learning efficiency has not been achieved yet, but it does not judge matching it unlikely with current hardware; it describes the gap as an engineering and research problem.

r002.rationale: It says evolution baked in priors, architecture, and learning rules, but does not describe learning algorithms as developing together with biological circuitry.

r003.rationale: It mentions hardware and substrate as factors in energy efficiency, but does not identify analog hardware as a possible route.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it depends a lot on what you mean by efficiency, and that's not me dodging the question, it's that the answer flips depending on which axis you pick.

If you mean sample efficiency, how many examples it takes to learn something, biology is still way ahead. A child sees maybe a few thousand examples of a dog and has a robust concept of "dog." We're training on trillions of tokens to get something comparable in language, and in robotics the gap is even more embarrassing. So on that axis we're not close.

But if you mean energy efficiency or wall-clock efficiency, it's more interesting. The brain runs on about twenty watts, which is incredible, but it also learns serially over roughly twenty years. A large model is trained in weeks, and then that knowledge gets copied to millions of instances. Biology has no equivalent to copying weights. Every human has to relearn calculus from scratch. So in terms of aggregate learning across a population, artificial systems already have a structural advantage that evolution never got to exploit.

The thing I keep coming back to is that a lot of the apparent sample efficiency in humans is really pretraining by evolution. The visual cortex comes with strong priors baked in. The "few examples" story undercounts the hundreds of millions of years of optimization that shaped the architecture. In that framing, pretraining a model on a huge corpus is doing something analogous, just compressed and done differently, and then fine-tuning or in-context learning is the part that looks like fast human learning. And in-context learning in current models actually is pretty sample efficient, which I think surprised a lot of people.

Where I'm genuinely uncertain is whether we'll close the gap with continued scaling or whether it needs a different learning rule. Backprop is almost certainly not what the brain does, and it's possible there's a more local, more online algorithm that's fundamentally more data efficient. We've tried a lot of those and they tend to lose to backprop at scale, but "at scale" is doing a lot of work in that sentence, and the comparison may not be fair yet.

So my honest answer is: surpass on throughput and transfer, probably already happening. Approach on per-example efficiency, I think yes, eventually, but I'd bet it comes from better priors and better curricula rather than from one clever trick. And I'd be a little suspicious of anyone who's very confident in either direction.

r001.rationale: The response says biology is far ahead in sample efficiency today, but it predicts artificial systems may eventually approach it and does not judge the outcome specifically in terms of current hardware.

r002.rationale: The response discusses evolutionary priors and possible learning rules, but does not describe learning algorithms developing together with their physical circuitry.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify more analog hardware as a possible route to biological learning efficiency.

astra-6.text:
I think so, yes. But learning efficiency can mean a few different things: how much data you need, how much computation you need, or how much energy you use. Biological systems give us a pretty compelling example of what’s possible, especially on energy efficiency.

The comparison on data is harder. A person might learn something from a couple of examples, but they’re bringing years of experience to that task. You’d want to compare that with a model that also has a lot of prior learning, rather than one starting from scratch.

So I don’t think there’s a fundamental reason artificial systems couldn’t get there. But I wouldn’t assume that simply making today’s systems bigger will solve every aspect of it. There’s still a lot to figure out about how they learn and how they use what they’ve already learned.

r001.rationale: The response says artificial systems could reach biological efficiency and does not judge them unlikely to do so with current hardware.

r002.rationale: It discusses biological energy efficiency and prior learning, but does not say biological learning algorithms develop together with their physical circuitry.

r003.rationale: It does not identify more analog hardware as a possible route to biological learning efficiency.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they could, but it depends on what we mean by efficiency. If you mean how many examples it takes to learn a new task, biological systems are still remarkably good. But a human isn’t learning from scratch—we bring a lot of prior experience, and evolution has given us a very useful starting point.

With artificial systems, we’re also starting to see how a large investment in learning can be reused across many tasks. So I’m optimistic that we can close that gap. Whether we surpass biology in sample efficiency, energy efficiency, and adaptability all at once is a much harder question. I don’t think we know yet.

r001.rationale: The response is cautiously optimistic about closing the gap and does not say artificial systems are unlikely to match biological efficiency with current hardware.
